items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Harold Pinter
items.stem: In Pinter's Birthday Party, Stanley is given a birthday present. What is it ?

structured.lead: In Pinter's Birthday Party, Stanley is given a birthday present. What is it ?
structured.options_hint: A toy A piano A drum A violin

items.explanation: In Act I of Harold Pinter's comedy of menace The Birthday Party (1958), Meg and Lulu present the reclusive former pianist Stanley Webber with a boy's toy drum and drumsticks as a birthday gift, which he beats with growing frenzy and terror as the act ends.

items.title: Q2 · June 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: How does Lord Jim end ?

structured.lead: How does Lord Jim end ?
structured.options_hint: Jim is shot through the chest by Doramin

options: Jim is shot through the chest by Doramin.
Jim kills himself with a last unflinching glance.
Jim answers "the call of exalted egoism" and betrays Jewel.
items.explanation: At the end of Joseph Conrad's Lord Jim (1900), after Dain Waris is killed in Gentleman Brown's treacherous attack, Jim voluntarily walks to the grieving chieftain Doramin and is shot fatally through the chest.

structured.lead: Where I lacked a political purpose, I wrote lifeless books." To which of the following authors can we attribute the above admission ?
structured.options_hint: Graham Greene George Orwell Charles Morg

items.explanation: In his famous 1946 essay 'Why I Write,' George Orwell reflected on his literary career and admitted that 'it is invariably where I lacked a political purpose that I wrote lifeless books and was betrayed into purple passages, sentences without meaning, decorative adjectives and humbug generally.'

items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit I: Drama · Richard Brinsley Sheridan

structured.lead:

structured.options_hint: Stephen Spender Malcolm Bradbury Lionel

items.explanation: In his essay 'On the Teaching of Modern Literature' (collected in Beyond Culture, 1965), American literary critic Lionel Trilling famously defined the characteristic theme of Modernism as 'the disenchantment of our culture with culture itself.'

Still flutters there, the sole unquiet thing."
The above lines are quoted from
structured.options_hint: Tintern Abbey Revisited Michael Frost at

items.explanation: These lines are from Samuel Taylor Coleridge's conversation poem 'Frost at Midnight' (1798), in which the speaker sits awake beside his cradled infant son Hartley in a silent cottage and watches the fluttering 'stranger'—a thin film of soot on the fireplace grate.

items.title: Q6 · June 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Which one of the following modern poems employs ottava rima ?

structured.lead: Which one of the following modern poems employs ottava rima ?
structured.options_hint: Among School Children Praise of Limeston

items.explanation: W. B. Yeats's modernist poem 'Among School Children' (collected in The Tower, 1928) is composed of eight stanzas in ottava rima—an eight-line iambic pentameter stanza rhyming abababcc—a form Yeats also employed in 'Sailing to Byzantium.'

structured.lead: Samuel Pepys kept his diary from

items.explanation: Restoration naval administrator Samuel Pepys kept his celebrated private diary in shorthand from January 1, 1660 to May 31, 1669, recording vivid eyewitness accounts of the Restoration of Charles II, the Great Plague of 1665, and the Great Fire of London in 1666.

items.title: Q10 · June 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: In the Defence of Poetry, what did Sydney attribute to poetry ?

structured.lead:
In the Defence of Poetry, what did
Sydney attribute to poetry ?
structured.options_hint: A magical power whereby poetry plays tri

options: A magical power whereby poetry plays tricks on the reader
A divine power whereby poetry transmits a message from God to the reader
A moral power whereby poetry encourages the reader to evaluate virtuous models
A realistic power that cannot be made to seem like mere illusion and trickery
items.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry / The Defence of Poesy (1595), Sir Philip Sidney defends poetry against Puritan attacks by attributing to it a supreme moral power: unlike abstract philosophy or factual history, poetry creates vivid, delightful models of virtue that move readers to noble action.

items.explanation: In his verse satire An Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot (1735), Alexander Pope includes two famous satirical portraits of contemporary figures: Joseph Addison as 'Atticus' (who could 'damn with faint praise') and John, Lord Hervey as the effeminate courtier 'Sporus.'

items.title: Q13 · June 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which of these plays by Shakespeare does not use 'cross-dressing' as a device ?

structured.lead: Which of these plays by Shakespeare does not use 'cross-dressing' as a device ?
structured.options_hint: You Like It Julius Caeser Cymbeline Two

items.explanation: Shakespeare frequently used female-to-male cross-dressing in his comedies and romances—Rosalind as Ganymede in As You Like It, Imogen as Fidele in Cymbeline, and Julia as Sebastian in The Two Gentlemen of Verona—whereas his Roman tragedy Julius Caesar (1599) does not employ this device.

items.title: Q15 · June 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding is a classic statement of _________ Philosophy

structured.lead:
Locke's Essay Concerning Human
Understanding is a classic statement of _________ Philosophy
structured.options_hint: Aesthetic Empiricist Nationalist Realist

items.explanation: John Locke's An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) is the foundational statement of British Empiricist philosophy, rejecting the doctrine of innate ideas and arguing that the mind at birth is a tabula rasa (blank slate) shaped entirely by sensory experience and reflection.

items.title: Q16 · June 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · Michel Foucault
items.stem: "Power circulates in all directions, to and from all social levels, at all times." Who said this ?

structured.lead: "Power circulates in all directions, to and from all social levels, at all times." Who said this ?
structured.options_hint: Edward Said Michel Foucault Jacques Derr

items.explanation: In Discipline and Punish (1975) and The History of Sexuality (1976), French theorist Michel Foucault rejected the traditional top-down model of sovereign power, arguing that power is not held exclusively by a ruling class but circulates in all directions across all social levels and discourses.

structured.options_hint: Robert Lowell Walt Whitman Wallace Steve

items.explanation: In Section 52, the concluding section of 'Song of Myself' in Leaves of Grass (1855), American poet Walt Whitman famously celebrates his untamed, democratic poetic voice: 'I too am not a bit tamed, I too am untranslatable, / I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world.'

items.title: Q22 · June 2013 (Paper II)

structured.lead: The etymological meaning of the word "trope" is
structured.options_hint: gesture turning mirror desire

items.explanation: The word 'trope' derives from the Greek noun tropos, meaning a 'turn,' 'direction,' or 'way' (from the verb trepein, 'to turn'), referring to a figure of speech in which a word or phrase is turned from its literal meaning to an imaginative or figurative sense.

items.title: Q23 · June 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem: Who among the following English poets defined poetic imagination as "a repetition in the finite mind of the eternal act of creation in the infinite 'I AM' " ?

structured.lead:
Who among the following English poets defined poetic imagination as
"a repetition in the finite mind of the eternal act of creation in the infinite
'I AM' " ?
structured.options_hint: Blake Wordsworth Coleridge Shelley

items.explanation: In Chapter 13 of Biographia Literaria (1817), Samuel Taylor Coleridge famously distinguished between Primary and Secondary Imagination, defining the Primary Imagination as 'the living Power and prime Agent of all human Perception, and as a repetition in the finite mind of the eternal act of creation in the infinite I AM.'

items.explanation: Sir Thomas Browne's spiritual testament Religio Medici ('The Religion of a Doctor,' 1643) meditates on Christian faith, charity, and God's providence; while the official UGC key marks it as a story of providential experiences, critics also widely note how the work celebrates Browne's love of mystery and wonder ('I love to lose myself in a mystery, to pursue my Reason to an O altitudo!').

structured.options_hint: Enumeration Antanagoge Parataxis Hypotax

items.explanation: In classical rhetoric, 'enumeration' (enumeratio) is the device of listing or detailing multiple parts, causes, or attributes of a subject one after another—here, cataloguing the beloved's eyes, hair, nose, cheeks, and lips for rhetorical emphasis.

items.explanation: Unlike Michel de Montaigne's intimate, subjective, and conversational essays, Francis Bacon's Essays (1597, 1612, 1625) are 'dispersed meditations' written in a terse, objective, and aphoristic style that distils accumulated public and worldly wisdom.

items.explanation: British statesman and novelist Benjamin Disraeli coined the phrase in his Condition-of-England novel Sybil, or The Two Nations (1845), describing industrial Britain as divided into two alienated nations—'the Rich and the Poor'—between whom there is no sympathy orshared understanding.

items.explanation: In the General Prologue to The Canterbury Tales, Geoffrey Chaucer describes the corrupt, worldly Friar Huberd as 'a noble post [pillar] unto his ordre,' using verbal irony to praise a mendicant who actually sells easy absolution for bribes and shuns the poor in favour of wealthy patrons.

items.explanation: First staged at London's Royal Court Theatre in May 1956, John Osborne's Look Back in Anger—set in Jimmy and Alison Porter's cramped, working-class Midlands flat—pioneered post-war British 'kitchen-sink drama,' which replaced polite drawing-room comedy with gritty domestic realism.

structured.options_hint: Blanche Ingram Brocklehurst Sir John Riv

items.explanation: In Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre (1847), the hypocritical clergyman Mr. Brocklehurst, supervisor of the Lowood charity school, uses stern evangelical religion to justify starving, freezing, and shearing the hair of the orphan girls to mortify their 'vile bodies' while his own daughters dress in silk and furs.

items.title: Q48 · June 2013 (Paper II)

items.stem: Which Romantic poet defined a slave as 'a person perverted into a thing' ?

structured.lead: Which Romantic poet defined a slave as 'a person perverted into a thing' ?
structured.options_hint: Blake Coleridge Keats Shelley

items.explanation: Samuel Taylor Coleridge, a lifelong opponent of slavery and the slave trade, defined a slave in his philosophical and political writings as 'a Person perverted into a Thing'—a moral human agent degraded by law and tyranny into mere chattel property.
